posts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
posts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
posts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

posts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
posts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
posts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

posts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
posts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
posts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

posts.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
posts.subtitle: BFS explores graphs level by level using a queue — the key to shortest paths and level-order problems.
posts.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

posts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
posts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
posts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

posts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
posts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
posts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

posts.title: Cell-Based Architectures: Designing Fault Isolation Boundaries for Million-User Apps
posts.subtitle: Design and implement cell-based routing using Spring Cloud Gateway to limit system blast radius.
posts.brief: As microservice architectures scale, a single outage in a core service can cascade across the entire system. Cell-Based Architecture mitigates this by partitioning the entire system into small, self-contained, independent units called cells. This guide outlines their routing mechanics and provides a custom Spring Cloud Gateway filter for cell-based traffic distribution.

posts.title: Concurrency Models: Actor Model vs. Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
posts.subtitle: An in-depth mathematical and practical comparison of the Actor Model and CSP concurrency patterns in Java.
posts.brief: Shared-memory multithreading using manual locks is notoriously difficult to scale and debug. To avoid race conditions and deadlocks, modern platforms use message-passing concurrency models. This guide compares the Actor Model (used in Erlang and Akka/Pekko) with Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, used in Go) and provides full Java implementations for both.

posts.title: Cyclic Sort: Find Missing and Duplicate Numbers in O(n) Time, O(1) Space
posts.subtitle: Place every number at its correct index in one sweep — then scan for mismatches. No HashSet, no extra memory.
posts.brief: If an array holds n numbers in range [1, n], each number belongs at index `num - 1`. Cyclic sort places every element at its correct index in O(n) time using O(1) space — then a single scan reveals every missing and duplicate number. Five interview problems, one technique.

posts.title: DFS — Depth-First Search: Go Deep Before Going Wide
posts.subtitle: DFS explores graphs by going as deep as possible before backtracking — the key to cycle detection and path search.
posts.brief: DFS explores a graph by diving as deep as possible along each path before backtracking, using a call stack (recursion) or an explicit stack. It is the go-to algorithm for cycle detection, path finding, topological sort, and connected components. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Watch for StackOverflow on deep graphs — use iterative DFS instead.

posts.title: Algorithms for AI: Trie, Graph Sorting, and K-Way Merge for LLM Systems
posts.subtitle: Master the core algorithms that power LLM token filtering, agent dependency planning, and hybrid search retrieval.
posts.brief: Generative AI relies heavily on classic computer science algorithms under the hood. In this guide, we explore how to implement Trie prefix filtering for constrained model decoding, Topological Sort for multi-agent scheduling, and K-Way Merge for merging dense and lexical search rankings.

posts.title: Domain-Driven Design (DDD): Designing Aggregates, Value Objects, and Context Boundaries
posts.subtitle: Master Domain-Driven Design (DDD) by learning how to enforce domain invariants using Aggregates and Value Objects in Java.
posts.brief: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) shifts the focus of software development from database schemas to core business logic. By implementing a rich domain model using Entities, Value Objects, and Aggregate Roots, we protect business invariants directly inside our code. This guide contrasts anemic domain models with rich DDD patterns in Java.

posts.title: Dynamic Programming Patterns: Solving the 0/1 Knapsack and LCS Series
posts.subtitle: Master the 0/1 Knapsack, LCS, and Edit Distance DP patterns with full Java solutions.
posts.brief: Dynamic Programming (DP) resolves complex optimization problems by breaking them down into overlapping subproblems, storing results to prevent redundant calculations. This guide introduces the core DP patterns and implements 0/1 Knapsack, LCS, and Edit Distance in Java.

posts.title: Strategy Design Pattern: Simplifying Software Design
posts.subtitle: Stop writing massive if-else statements. The Strategy Pattern allows you to swap algorithms at runtime. We explain it with a Payment Processing exampl
posts.brief: The Strategy Pattern replaces giant `if-else` or `switch` blocks with a family of interchangeable algorithm classes. Each strategy is a self-contained unit that can be swapped at runtime without touching the client code. The result: Open/Closed Principle compliance and dramatically easier testing.

posts.title: Fast and Slow Pointer: Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm Explained
posts.subtitle: Detect cycles, find their starts, and locate list midpoints — all in O(n) time and O(1) space.
posts.brief: Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps through a linked structure. If they ever meet, a cycle exists. Then reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time — where they meet next is the cycle's start node. This single algorithm, invented by Robert Floyd in the 1960s, solves cycle detection, cycle start finding, linked list midpoint, and the Happy Number problem — all in O(n) time with O(1) space.

posts.title: How It Works: Thread Safety Internals of Java's ConcurrentHashMap
posts.subtitle: Explore volatile reads, Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loops, bucket-head locking, and parallel resizing in Java's map.
posts.brief: Java's `ConcurrentHashMap` achieves high read throughput and thread-safe writes by avoiding table-level locks. It utilizes lock-free `volatile` node reads and isolates write locking to individual bucket heads, allowing separate threads to write to different slots concurrently.

posts.title: How JVM Garbage Collection Works: Types, Memory Impact, and Tuning
posts.subtitle: From Minor GC to ZGC: how each Java garbage collector manages heap memory and what it means for your application's latency and throughput.
posts.brief: JVM garbage collection automatically reclaims unused heap memory, but every algorithm makes a different trade-off between throughput, latency, and memory footprint. The default G1GC targets 200ms pause goals and works well for most services. For sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps, use ZGC (Java 15+). For pure batch throughput, Parallel GC wins. Understanding heap regions — Eden, Survivor, Old Gen, Metaspace — tells you why `OutOfMemoryError` happens, what triggers a full GC, and which JVM flags to tune first.

posts.brief: This is the code companion to the [Parking Lot System Design](./lld-parking-lot-system) post. We implement the core classes (`ParkingLot`, `ParkingSpot`, `Ticket`) in Java, apply the **Singleton**, **Factory**, and **Strategy** patterns, and use a Min-Heap to find the nearest available spot in O(log n).

posts.title: In-Place Reversal of a Linked List: The 3-Pointer Dance Every Interviewer Expects
posts.subtitle: Master prev, curr, and next — the three-pointer pattern that unlocks full reversal, sub-list reversal, and K-group rotation in O(1) space.
posts.brief: Reversing a linked list in O(1) space requires three pointers — `prev`, `curr`, and `next`. Each step: save `next`, flip `curr.next` to point backward, advance both `prev` and `curr`. Learn this once and you unlock four reversal variants that appear constantly in interviews.

posts.title: Java 14 to 17: Records, Sealed Classes, Text Blocks, and Pattern Matching
posts.subtitle: Records eliminated boilerplate. Sealed classes enforced type hierarchies. Pattern matching removed redundant casts. Java 17 LTS made it stable.
posts.brief: Java 14–17 ran a deliberate four-release preview-to-stable conveyor belt. Records replaced 50-line POJOs with one line. Text blocks ended escape-sequence chaos in multi-line strings. Sealed classes turned "please only subclass these types" comments into compiler errors. Pattern matching `instanceof` eliminated the check-then-cast antipattern. All four features are stable in Java 17 LTS and work together as a cohesive system for expressing immutable value types and finite domain hierarchies. Upgrade path: records for DTOs immediately, sealed classes for domain hierarchies, text blocks for all inline SQL/JSON in tests — in that order.

posts.title: Java 21 to 25: Virtual Threads, Pattern Matching, and Structured Concurrency
posts.subtitle: Virtual threads replace thread pools for I/O work. Structured concurrency replaces CompletableFuture. Java 21 LTS is the biggest release since Java 8.
posts.brief: Java 21 LTS makes virtual threads a production-ready replacement for bounded thread pools — your `newFixedThreadPool(200)` can become `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` and handle 10× the concurrency with no architectural changes. Pattern switch with guards replaces verbose `instanceof` chains. `SequencedCollection` adds `getFirst()`/`getLast()` to `List` and `LinkedHashSet`. Structured concurrency cancels sibling tasks on failure — something `CompletableFuture.allOf()` never did. The single biggest gotcha: `synchronized` over I/O **pins** a virtual thread to its carrier OS thread, wiping out every benefit. Use `ReentrantLock` instead.

posts.title: Java 8 to 11: Lambdas, Streams, Modules, and the End of Boilerplate
posts.subtitle: How lambdas, streams, Optional, and Java 9 modules transformed Java from verbose boilerplate to expressive, maintainable code
posts.brief: Java 8 introduced the most impactful set of language features in Java's history — lambdas eliminated anonymous inner classes, streams replaced imperative loops, and Optional made null handling explicit. Java 9's module system drew a boundary around the JDK itself. Java 10's `var` removed redundant type declarations. Java 11 LTS added unicode-aware string methods, a built-in HTTP/2 client, and became the migration baseline for most enterprise teams. Understanding *which pain each feature removes* is what separates engineers who adopt features on principle from engineers who adopt them to solve real problems.

posts.title: Java 8 to Java 25: How Java Evolved from Boilerplate to a Modern Language
posts.subtitle: Every major Java feature from 8 to 25 — lambdas, records, sealed classes, virtual threads, pattern matching, and what they replace
posts.brief: Java went from the most verbose mainstream language to one of the most expressive. Lambdas killed anonymous inner classes. Records killed POJOs. Virtual threads killed thread pools for I/O work. Sealed classes killed unchecked inheritance. Each feature in this guide exists to eliminate a specific category of pain — and understanding *why* makes you a better engineer on any version of Java.

posts.title: K-Way Merge Pattern: Merge K Sorted Sequences with a Min-Heap
posts.subtitle: A min-heap tracks one pointer per sorted list. Pop the global minimum, advance that list's pointer, repeat.
posts.brief: K-Way Merge uses a min-heap with exactly one entry per sorted input list. Each entry stores the current element's value plus the coordinates to find the next element in that list. Pop the minimum (global smallest), append it to output, push the next element from the same list. Repeat until the heap is empty. Time: O(N log K) for N total elements across K lists.

Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees optimize both operations to $O(\log N)$ time. This guide breaks down their core intuition, visualizes their internal layouts, and provides complete Java implementations.

posts.subtitle: Why modern teams keep one golden branch releasable, ship behind toggles, and handle hotfixes without GitFlow drama.

posts.title: Sliding Window Technique: From O(n·k) Scans to O(n) in One Pass
posts.subtitle: Eliminate redundant subarray re-scanning by maintaining a running aggregate across an expanding and shrinking boundary.
posts.brief: Instead of recomputing a subarray aggregate from scratch on every shift, maintain it incrementally — add the incoming element, remove the outgoing element. For a fixed window this costs O(1) per shift. For a variable window, expand the right boundary until a condition is met, then shrink the left boundary until the condition breaks. Every element enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n) total regardless of window size.

posts.title: Tarjan’s Algorithm: Finding Strongly Connected Components (SCC) step-by-step
posts.subtitle: Master graph partitioning by deriving and implementing Tarjan's linear-time SCC algorithm in Java.
posts.brief: In directed graphs, a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) is a maximal subset of vertices where every vertex is reachable from any other vertex in the subset. Finding these components is crucial for resolving circular dependencies. Tarjan's algorithm finds all SCCs in a single Depth-First Search (DFS) pass, achieving an optimal $O(V + E)$ time complexity. This guide details its mechanics, mathematical models, and provides a full Java implementation.

posts.title: Top K Elements Pattern: Find the Best K Without Sorting Everything
posts.subtitle: Maintain a min-heap of size K. Anything smaller than the current minimum gets evicted immediately.
posts.brief: To find the top K largest elements, maintain a **min-heap of size K**. For every new element, push it onto the heap. If the heap exceeds K, evict the minimum. After processing all N elements, the heap holds exactly the K largest. O(N log K) time — orders of magnitude faster than sorting when K is small.

posts.title: Tries (Prefix Trees): The Data Structure Behind Autocomplete
posts.subtitle: A Trie stores strings character by character — enabling O(L) prefix queries no HashMap can match.
posts.brief: A Trie stores strings character by character in a tree, so every string sharing a common prefix shares those nodes. Insert and search are O(L) where L is the word length. Tries beat HashMaps on prefix queries — `startsWith` in O(L) with zero collision overhead. The canonical interview implementation uses a 26-element `children` array and an `isEndOfWord` flag.

posts.title: Two Heaps Pattern: Find the Median of a Data Stream Without Sorting
posts.subtitle: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. The median lives at the boundary.
posts.brief: Two Heaps partitions a stream into two sorted halves. A max-heap holds everything below the median; a min-heap holds everything above it. Keep the heaps size-balanced and you can read the median from either top in O(1) — no sorting needed, ever.

posts.title: Two Pointer Technique: Solving Pair and Partition Problems in O(n)
posts.subtitle: Collapse O(n²) pair-search problems to O(n) by converging two index boundaries on a sorted array.
posts.brief: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end of a sorted array. Move them toward each other based on a comparison condition. Every classic pair/partition problem that naively runs in O(n²) collapses to O(n) with this one idea — and mastering it unlocks Three Sum, Container With Most Water, and dozens of interview problems in one mental model.

posts.brief: Altering database schemas in a high-traffic production system without downtime requires the Expand-Contract pattern. Instead of changing a column in place, we add a new column (Expand), double-write to both columns via the application (Transition), backfill historical data, and finally remove the old column (Contract). This guide details this lifecycle with full Spring Boot and Liquibase snippets.

ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
posts.subtitle: From WAL and MVCC to fsync and isolation levels — the internals behind every ACID guarantee in PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
posts.brief: ACID is four orthogonal guarantees that every SQL transaction must provide. Atomicity says all-or-nothing: PostgreSQL implements it via WAL rollback; MySQL InnoDB via undo logs. Consistency says constraints always hold: the database rejects any write that violates a `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `NOT NULL`. Isolation says concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states: PostgreSQL uses MVCC + Serializable Snapshot Isolation; MySQL InnoDB uses MVCC + Two-Phase Locking. Durability says committed data survives crashes: every major database writes to a write-ahead log and calls `fsync` before acknowledging a commit. Know which property protects which failure class — and know the configuration knobs that let you trade durability for throughput when the workload permits.

Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

posts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
posts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

posts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
posts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
posts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

journey.label: Java
journey.description: Learn Java as a connected topic across chapters, concepts, simulations, and interview reasoning.

articles.title: How It Works: Thread Safety Internals of Java's ConcurrentHashMap
articles.brief: Java's `ConcurrentHashMap` achieves high read throughput and thread-safe writes by avoiding table-level locks. It utilizes lock-free `volatile` node reads and isolates write locking to individual bucket heads, allowing separate threads to write to different slots concurrently.

articles.title: Java 14 to 17: Records, Sealed Classes, Text Blocks, and Pattern Matching
articles.brief: Java 14–17 ran a deliberate four-release preview-to-stable conveyor belt. Records replaced 50-line POJOs with one line. Text blocks ended escape-sequence chaos in multi-line strings. Sealed classes turned "please only subclass these types" comments into compiler errors. Pattern matching `instanceof` eliminated the check-then-cast antipattern. All four features are stable in Java 17 LTS and work together as a cohesive system for expressing immutable value types and finite domain hierarchies. Upgrade path: records for DTOs immediately, sealed classes for domain hierarchies, text blocks for all inline SQL/JSON in tests — in that order.

articles.title: Java 21 to 25: Virtual Threads, Pattern Matching, and Structured Concurrency
articles.brief: Java 21 LTS makes virtual threads a production-ready replacement for bounded thread pools — your `newFixedThreadPool(200)` can become `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` and handle 10× the concurrency with no architectural changes. Pattern switch with guards replaces verbose `instanceof` chains. `SequencedCollection` adds `getFirst()`/`getLast()` to `List` and `LinkedHashSet`. Structured concurrency cancels sibling tasks on failure — something `CompletableFuture.allOf()` never did. The single biggest gotcha: `synchronized` over I/O **pins** a virtual thread to its carrier OS thread, wiping out every benefit. Use `ReentrantLock` instead.

articles.title: Java 8 to 11: Lambdas, Streams, Modules, and the End of Boilerplate
articles.brief: Java 8 introduced the most impactful set of language features in Java's history — lambdas eliminated anonymous inner classes, streams replaced imperative loops, and Optional made null handling explicit. Java 9's module system drew a boundary around the JDK itself. Java 10's `var` removed redundant type declarations. Java 11 LTS added unicode-aware string methods, a built-in HTTP/2 client, and became the migration baseline for most enterprise teams. Understanding *which pain each feature removes* is what separates engineers who adopt features on principle from engineers who adopt them to solve real problems.

articles.title: Java 8 to Java 25: How Java Evolved from Boilerplate to a Modern Language
articles.brief: Java went from the most verbose mainstream language to one of the most expressive. Lambdas killed anonymous inner classes. Records killed POJOs. Virtual threads killed thread pools for I/O work. Sealed classes killed unchecked inheritance. Each feature in this guide exists to eliminate a specific category of pain — and understanding *why* makes you a better engineer on any version of Java.

articles.title: Java Memory Model Demystified: Stack vs. Heap
articles.brief: Java memory is split into two main areas: the **Stack** for method execution frames and primitives, and the **Heap** for all objects. Understanding their differences is essential for avoiding stack overflow errors, memory leaks, and garbage collection pauses.

articles.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
articles.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

articles.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
articles.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

articles.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
articles.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

articles.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
articles.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

articles.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
articles.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

articles.title: Cell-Based Architectures: Designing Fault Isolation Boundaries for Million-User Apps
articles.brief: As microservice architectures scale, a single outage in a core service can cascade across the entire system. Cell-Based Architecture mitigates this by partitioning the entire system into small, self-contained, independent units called cells. This guide outlines their routing mechanics and provides a custom Spring Cloud Gateway filter for cell-based traffic distribution.

articles.title: Concurrency Models: Actor Model vs. Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
articles.brief: Shared-memory multithreading using manual locks is notoriously difficult to scale and debug. To avoid race conditions and deadlocks, modern platforms use message-passing concurrency models. This guide compares the Actor Model (used in Erlang and Akka/Pekko) with Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, used in Go) and provides full Java implementations for both.

articles.title: Cyclic Sort: Find Missing and Duplicate Numbers in O(n) Time, O(1) Space
articles.brief: If an array holds n numbers in range [1, n], each number belongs at index `num - 1`. Cyclic sort places every element at its correct index in O(n) time using O(1) space — then a single scan reveals every missing and duplicate number. Five interview problems, one technique.

articles.title: DFS — Depth-First Search: Go Deep Before Going Wide
articles.brief: DFS explores a graph by diving as deep as possible along each path before backtracking, using a call stack (recursion) or an explicit stack. It is the go-to algorithm for cycle detection, path finding, topological sort, and connected components. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Watch for StackOverflow on deep graphs — use iterative DFS instead.

articles.title: Algorithms for AI: Trie, Graph Sorting, and K-Way Merge for LLM Systems
articles.brief: Generative AI relies heavily on classic computer science algorithms under the hood. In this guide, we explore how to implement Trie prefix filtering for constrained model decoding, Topological Sort for multi-agent scheduling, and K-Way Merge for merging dense and lexical search rankings.

articles.title: Domain-Driven Design (DDD): Designing Aggregates, Value Objects, and Context Boundaries
articles.brief: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) shifts the focus of software development from database schemas to core business logic. By implementing a rich domain model using Entities, Value Objects, and Aggregate Roots, we protect business invariants directly inside our code. This guide contrasts anemic domain models with rich DDD patterns in Java.

articles.title: Dynamic Programming Patterns: Solving the 0/1 Knapsack and LCS Series
articles.brief: Dynamic Programming (DP) resolves complex optimization problems by breaking them down into overlapping subproblems, storing results to prevent redundant calculations. This guide introduces the core DP patterns and implements 0/1 Knapsack, LCS, and Edit Distance in Java.

articles.title: Strategy Design Pattern: Simplifying Software Design
articles.brief: The Strategy Pattern replaces giant `if-else` or `switch` blocks with a family of interchangeable algorithm classes. Each strategy is a self-contained unit that can be swapped at runtime without touching the client code. The result: Open/Closed Principle compliance and dramatically easier testing.

articles.title: Fast and Slow Pointer: Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm Explained
articles.brief: Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps through a linked structure. If they ever meet, a cycle exists. Then reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time — where they meet next is the cycle's start node. This single algorithm, invented by Robert Floyd in the 1960s, solves cycle detection, cycle start finding, linked list midpoint, and the Happy Number problem — all in O(n) time with O(1) space.

articles.title: How JVM Garbage Collection Works: Types, Memory Impact, and Tuning
articles.brief: JVM garbage collection automatically reclaims unused heap memory, but every algorithm makes a different trade-off between throughput, latency, and memory footprint. The default G1GC targets 200ms pause goals and works well for most services. For sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps, use ZGC (Java 15+). For pure batch throughput, Parallel GC wins. Understanding heap regions — Eden, Survivor, Old Gen, Metaspace — tells you why `OutOfMemoryError` happens, what triggers a full GC, and which JVM flags to tune first.

articles.title: Implement LLD for Parking Lot: Code Walkthrough
articles.brief: This is the code companion to the [Parking Lot System Design](./lld-parking-lot-system) post. We implement the core classes (`ParkingLot`, `ParkingSpot`, `Ticket`) in Java, apply the **Singleton**, **Factory**, and **Strategy** patterns, and use a Min-Heap to find the nearest available spot in O(log n).

articles.title: In-Place Reversal of a Linked List: The 3-Pointer Dance Every Interviewer Expects
articles.brief: Reversing a linked list in O(1) space requires three pointers — `prev`, `curr`, and `next`. Each step: save `next`, flip `curr.next` to point backward, advance both `prev` and `curr`. Learn this once and you unlock four reversal variants that appear constantly in interviews.

articles.title: K-Way Merge Pattern: Merge K Sorted Sequences with a Min-Heap
articles.brief: K-Way Merge uses a min-heap with exactly one entry per sorted input list. Each entry stores the current element's value plus the coordinates to find the next element in that list. Pop the minimum (global smallest), append it to output, push the next element from the same list. Repeat until the heap is empty. Time: O(N log K) for N total elements across K lists.

articles.title: Liskov Substitution Principle Demystified: The Heart of Polymorphism
articles.brief: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) mandates that subclasses must be substitutable for their superclasses without changing the correctness of the program. It shifts our understanding of inheritance from syntax (IS-A) to behavior (behaves-like).

articles.title: Low-Level Design for an AI Agent Orchestration Engine: Designing a Stateful Execution Framework
articles.brief: In this guide, we design a stateful, graph-based AI agent execution engine in Java using clean object-oriented principles. By structuring execution as nodes and edges over a shared state, we prevent memory leaks, manage complex routing, and create a highly extensible framework.

articles.title: LLD for Tic-Tac-Toe: Designing an Extensible OOP Game
articles.brief: Tic-Tac-Toe looks trivial — until the interviewer says "make it N×N with P players and pluggable winning rules." The key design decisions: a Board abstracted from piece identity, a Strategy Pattern for win conditions, and a Factory for player creation. Getting these right is the interview objective.

articles.title: Low-Level Design: Building a Thread-Safe In-Memory Pub-Sub Queue
articles.brief: Building an in-memory message queue is a premier LLD problem testing multithreaded design. By combining the observer pattern with Java reentrant locks, conditions, and concurrent atomic offsets, we implement a thread-safe broker that decouples producers and consumers.

articles.title: Low-Level Design: Designing a Vending Machine using the State Pattern
articles.brief: Designing a Vending Machine is a classic low-level design interview problem that tests state-driven logic. By using the GoF State Pattern, we avoid nested conditional blocks and build a modular, thread-safe system in Java Spring Boot.

articles.title: LLD for Ride Booking App: Designing Uber/Lyft
articles.brief: A ride-booking system (Uber/Lyft-style) needs three interleaved sub-systems: real-time driver location tracking (Observer Pattern), nearest-driver matching (geospatial query), and dynamic pricing (Strategy Pattern). Getting state transitions right — Requested → Accepted → InProgress → Completed — is the core LLD challenge.

articles.title: Merge Intervals Pattern: Solve Scheduling Problems with Sort and Sweep
articles.brief: Sort intervals by start time, then sweep left-to-right and merge any interval whose start ≤ the current running end. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. One pattern — three interview problems solved.

articles.title: Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees: Mastering Range Query Optimization
articles.brief: When dealing with dynamic arrays where elements are frequently updated and range queries (like sum or minimum) are continuously executed, a naive loop takes $O(N)$ time per query. Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees optimize both operations to $O(\log N)$ time. This guide breaks down their core intuition, visualizes their internal layouts, and provides complete Java implementations.

articles.title: Single Trunk Model Explained: Golden Branches, Feature Toggles, and Continuous Feature Delivery
articles.brief: The single trunk model exists to reduce integration pain, shorten feedback loops, and keep one golden branch always releasable. Teams make it work with strong CI, short-lived feature branches, feature toggles, and a hotfix process that fixes trunk first instead of forking release history.

articles.title: Sliding Window Technique: From O(n·k) Scans to O(n) in One Pass
articles.brief: Instead of recomputing a subarray aggregate from scratch on every shift, maintain it incrementally — add the incoming element, remove the outgoing element. For a fixed window this costs O(1) per shift. For a variable window, expand the right boundary until a condition is met, then shrink the left boundary until the condition breaks. Every element enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n) total regardless of window size.

articles.title: Tarjan’s Algorithm: Finding Strongly Connected Components (SCC) step-by-step
articles.brief: In directed graphs, a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) is a maximal subset of vertices where every vertex is reachable from any other vertex in the subset. Finding these components is crucial for resolving circular dependencies. Tarjan's algorithm finds all SCCs in a single Depth-First Search (DFS) pass, achieving an optimal $O(V + E)$ time complexity. This guide details its mechanics, mathematical models, and provides a full Java implementation.

articles.title: Top K Elements Pattern: Find the Best K Without Sorting Everything
articles.brief: To find the top K largest elements, maintain a **min-heap of size K**. For every new element, push it onto the heap. If the heap exceeds K, evict the minimum. After processing all N elements, the heap holds exactly the K largest. O(N log K) time — orders of magnitude faster than sorting when K is small.

articles.title: Tries (Prefix Trees): The Data Structure Behind Autocomplete
articles.brief: A Trie stores strings character by character in a tree, so every string sharing a common prefix shares those nodes. Insert and search are O(L) where L is the word length. Tries beat HashMaps on prefix queries — `startsWith` in O(L) with zero collision overhead. The canonical interview implementation uses a 26-element `children` array and an `isEndOfWord` flag.

articles.title: Two Heaps Pattern: Find the Median of a Data Stream Without Sorting
articles.brief: Two Heaps partitions a stream into two sorted halves. A max-heap holds everything below the median; a min-heap holds everything above it. Keep the heaps size-balanced and you can read the median from either top in O(1) — no sorting needed, ever.

articles.title: Two Pointer Technique: Solving Pair and Partition Problems in O(n)
articles.brief: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end of a sorted array. Move them toward each other based on a comparison condition. Every classic pair/partition problem that naively runs in O(n²) collapses to O(n) with this one idea — and mastering it unlocks Three Sum, Container With Most Water, and dozens of interview problems in one mental model.

articles.title: Zero-Downtime Schema Migrations: The Expand-Contract Pattern for Live Production DBs
articles.brief: Altering database schemas in a high-traffic production system without downtime requires the Expand-Contract pattern. Instead of changing a column in place, we add a new column (Expand), double-write to both columns via the application (Transition), backfill historical data, and finally remove the old column (Contract). This guide details this lifecycle with full Spring Boot and Liquibase snippets.

articles.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
articles.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

articles.title: Python Basics: Variables, Types, and Control Flow
articles.brief: Python variables are labels that point at objects — not typed boxes. The type lives with the object, not the variable. Master truthiness, f-strings, `for`/`while` loops, and the handful of pitfalls that trip up every developer coming from Java or JavaScript, and you'll write idiomatic Python from day one.

articles.title: Functions in Python: Parameters, Return Values, and Scope
articles.brief: Python functions are first-class objects, not just reusable blocks. They support keyword arguments, safe defaults with `None`, variadic `*args`/`**kwargs`, closures, and LEGB scope resolution. These five ideas are not advanced features — they are the foundation of everything from decorators to FastAPI route definitions.

articles.title: Pythonic Code: Idioms Every Developer Should Know
articles.brief: Writing `for i in range(len(arr)):` works, but Python veterans will flag it in your first code review. Idiomatic Python uses `enumerate`, `zip`, comprehensions, context managers, unpacking, the walrus operator, and truthiness checks — not because they're clever, but because they compress intent into the minimum readable form. Learn these 10+ idioms and your Python will look like it belongs in the language.
